title: Era 1: the S&P "TGA" engine (v10–v25)
hypothesis: Graph-topology and reversal signals on S&P 500 single names earn a daily edge.
question: Could a minimum-spanning-tree ("TGA") and cross-sectional reversal engine, layered with filters, an XGBoost gate and Kelly sizing, beat the market on daily S&P 500 data?
prior: Short-horizon reversal is one of the oldest documented anomalies (Lehmann 1990; Lo and MacKinlay 1990). Whether it survives costs in large caps today was the open question.
citations: Lehmann, B. (1990). Fads, Martingales, and Market Efficiency. QJE 105(1).
Lo, A. & MacKinlay, A. C. (1990). When Are Contrarian Profits Due to Stock Market Overreaction? RFS 3(2).
method: PIT S&P 500 universe, daily OHLCV, MOO T+1 fills at 7 bps.
v10–v17: MST engine plus layered filters; v18–v24: cross-sectional beta-neutral engine, XGBoost gate, quarter-Kelly, regime allocator with a momentum leg.
Frozen Phase-1 baseline: v24_combined_nodrl, Sharpe +0.602 on 2022-07 → 2026-04.
verdict_reason: Historical, not reproducible. A 2026-05 cache re-download (768 → 831 tickers) reshuffled every cross-sectional rank and the +0.602 no longer reproduces; v26 showed the engine's alpha is indistinguishable from zero and the baseline was carried by momentum.
lessons: Filter cascades (v16/v17/v20) cut the trade flow to nothing; a shock gate blocked entries exactly when the signal fired.
Intraday ATR stops fired 342 times at an average −4.07%; they were removed.
A result that moves with the ticker list is not an edge: record the data vintage with every number.
metrics_note: Numbers from the archived v24 spec (2022-07 → 2026-04, 768-ticker cache); not re-runnable.
footer: Research code is private; methods summarised below.
